en: Itivuttaka 41 Dukanipāta, Second Chapter Thus it was said by the Blessed One; having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, when the venerable Ānanda had understood that the Blessed One had risen from his seat and entered his dwelling, he approached the group of five monks. Having approached, he spoke thus to the group of five monks: “Friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling. You may do as you think fit. Then the venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down at one side. As he was sitting there, the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, the group of five monks has been well-instructed by the Blessed One. Venerable sir, it would be well if the Blessed One were to teach the Dhamma to the group of five monks; having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, the group of five monks will practice in accordance with the Dhamma. “It is hard for me, Ānanda, to teach the Dhamma to the group of five monks. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, the group of five monks has been well-instructed by me. Yet, Ānanda, if you so desire, you may approach the group of five monks and say to them: ‘Friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling. Friends, the Blessed One desires to dwell alone in seclusion. Friends, the Blessed One does not wish to speak much. “Yes, venerable sir,” the venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. Then he approached the group of five monks. Having approached, he spoke thus to the group of five monks: “Friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling. Friends, the Blessed One desires to dwell alone in seclusion. Friends, the Blessed One does not wish to speak much. “Indeed, friend Ānanda, the Blessed One has been well-instructed by us. Friend Ānanda, let the Blessed One rise from his seat and enter his dwelling; the Blessed One shall dwell alone in seclusion. Friend Ānanda, the Blessed One does not wish to speak much. Then the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then the group of five monks approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down at one side. As they were sitting there, the Blessed One spoke thus to the group of five monks: “Monks, these two extremes should not be followed by one who has gone forth into homelessness. What two? The pursuit of sensual pleasure in sense-objects, which is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unprofitable; and the pursuit of self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and unprofitable. Monks, the Tathāgata has abandoned both these extremes and has awakened to the middle way, which produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, higher knowledge, full enlightenment, and Nibbāna. And what, monks, is that middle way awakened to by the Tathāgata? It is the Noble Eightfold Path; that is to say: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is that middle way awakened to by the Tathāgata, which produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, higher knowledge, full enlightenment, and Nibbāna. Now, monks, this is the noble truth of suffering: birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering; union with what is displeasing is suffering; separation from what is pleasing is suffering; not to get what one wants is suffering; in short, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering. This, monks, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering: it is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for cessation of existence. This, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering: it is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, giving it up, relinquishing it, letting it go, and not relying on it. This, monks, is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering: it is this Noble Eightfold Path; that is to say: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. ‘This is the noble truth of suffering’—thus, monks, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light. ‘This noble truth of suffering must be fully understood’—thus, monks, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light. ‘This noble truth of suffering has been fully understood’—thus, monks, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light. ‘This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering’—thus, monks, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light. ‘This noble truth of the origin of suffering must be abandoned’—thus, monks, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light. ‘This noble truth of the origin of suffering has been abandoned’—thus, monks, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light. ‘This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering’—thus, monks, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light. ‘This noble truth of the cessation of suffering must be realized’—thus, monks, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light. ‘This noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized’—thus, monks, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light. ‘This is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—thus, monks, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light. ‘This noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering must be developed’—thus, monks, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light. ‘This noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering has been developed’—thus, monks, in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light. As long as, monks, this knowledge and vision of mine regarding these four noble truths, in their three phases and twelve aspects, was not thoroughly purified in this way, I did not claim to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. But when, monks, this knowledge and vision of mine regarding these four noble truths, in their three phases and twelve aspects, was thoroughly purified in this way, then I claimed to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans. The knowledge and vision arose in me: ‘Unshakable is my liberation of mind; this is my last birth; now there is no more renewed existence. When this was said, the venerable Koṇḍañña said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is clear to me; venerable sir, it is clear to me. “Therefore, Koṇḍañña, you have truly understood; therefore, Koṇḍañña, you have truly understood. Hence, Koṇḍañña, you are named ‘Aññā-Koṇḍañña’ (Koṇḍañña who has understood). And so, the venerable Aññā-Koṇḍañña became one of the stream-enterers, having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, fathomed the Dhamma, crossed over uncertainty, dispelled doubt, attained confidence, and became independent of others in the Teacher’s instruction. And the group of five monks, with the venerable Aññā-Koṇḍañña as their leader, became followers of the Dhamma.
The Discourse on the Loss of Wisdom.
This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant; so I have heard:
"Those beings, monks, are utterly lost who are deprived of noble wisdom."
In this very life they dwell in suffering, with vexation, despair, and fever;
and with the breakup of the body, after death, a bad destination is to be expected for them.
These beings, monks, are not fallen away, in that they have not fallen away from noble wisdom.
“They dwell in happiness in this very life— unafflicted, untroubled, and without fever—
and with the breakup of the body, after death, a happy destination is to be expected for them.
Thus the Blessed One spoke on this matter.
Regarding this, it is said:
"Behold the world together with its devas through the decline of wisdom."
Established in name-and-form,
one thinks, "This is the truth.
For wisdom is supreme in the world.
That which leads to penetration;
by means of which one rightly understands the complete destruction of birth and existence.
Both gods and humans yearn for those Buddhas who possess mindfulness and the wisdom of laughter.
"Of those who bear their final body.
This meaning was also spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
The fourth [sutta].
